editorial.headline: Mandatory Social Security: Closed to PMA, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This government-organised system of compulsory social protection is closed to PMA nationwide, and Bali records the same outcome even though its moratorium is not the stated reason.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering Bali, the answer begins with a hard boundary: this activity cannot be registered as PMA there today. That conclusion is not a Bali-only surprise. Nationally, Mandatory Social Security Activities is marked TERTUTUP, with a foreign-ownership maximum of 0%. In Bali, the status is likewise TERTUTUP. The provincial note classifies it as medium-high/high risk and says it is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, while directing that the position be verified for the particular address.

At its centre is the government’s financing and administration of compulsory social security. The scope encompasses social protection connected to health, accidents and unemployment, as well as pensions. It also reaches programmes dealing with income loss caused by maternity, temporary disability, widowhood and related circumstances. Read as a whole, the definition is about the public machinery behind mandated protection: funding and administering schemes intended to respond when health, work or family circumstances affect a person’s income. The key modifiers—compulsory, government-organised, financed and administered—are all essential to its institutional focus.

The registration fields reinforce that institutional character. Government is identified as the organiser, and the record provides no business scale open to this activity. There is consequently no stated business-scale route for treating it as an open business category, and no additional scale qualification appears elsewhere in the record. That is important for a founder reading only the activity title: the applicable scope is the funding and administration of compulsory schemes, and the record’s national PMA setting leaves no foreign ownership space within it. The absence of an open scale is a substantive part of the picture, not a detail to fill by assumption.

Bali’s detailed treatment must be read with equal precision. The province-wide permanent moratorium named in the record applies at the Low and Medium-Low risk levels. This activity, however, is recorded as medium-high/high risk and expressly described as not blocked by that moratorium. That does not turn it into an open Bali option. The Bali status remains TERTUTUP, and the record calls for verification by address. The clean conclusion is therefore narrow but decisive: the moratorium is not the reason given for the Bali outcome, yet a foreign-owned registration for this activity in Bali is closed today. Nationally, its 0% foreign-ownership maximum reaches the same result.
